survey: Alderdyke is a small fen town with a council, library, church, social club, newsletter, pumping station and field research works.
story: The field works have begun running a low, uneven cycle of machinery after midnight, while the pumping station's readings remain ordinary. edge.road: the west road out past the pumping station and the field works
edge.whatTheyFind: The road passes the works and reaches a white bridge over a narrow dyke. Beyond it the fields and ditches continue, with no houses or signs to distinguish them. At about 4.8 miles from town there is the same white bridge again, with the same chipped corner and bent railing. The road and fields carry on beyond it.

pages.title: Welcome to the Council Pages
pages.content:
WELCOME TO THE COUNCIL PAGES

Welcome to the Alderdyke Town Council website. This site is maintained by Oren Tebb, part-time clerk to the council.

The clerk is in attendance at the council office on Tuesday mornings from nine until twelve, and Thursday afternoons from two until half past four. Outside these hours, letters may be placed through the brass flap in the door.

Please note that the council office is situated on Harbour Street, near the coal yard. Visitors often ask why it is called Harbour Street when there has never been a harbour there, nor any boat traffic beyond the common fen lighters on the dyke. The name appears on maps as far back as 1842 and the council has never found cause to alter it.

> Ditches and Drains council.ad/ditches
> Minutes and Older Papers council.ad/minutes

pages.title: Ditches and Drains
pages.content:
DITCHES AND DRAINS

A reminder concerning the maintenance of roadside ditches and common watercourses across Alderdyke parish.

The roadside ditches along the north lane are the charge of adjacent landowners, whereas the main dyke running down toward the pumping station is kept by the district board. They are not cleared at the same season. Roadside ditches should be rodded and cleared of weed before the first hard frost, usually the middle of October. The main dyke is cleared later, in late November, once the autumn levels have settled.

The council minutes for 1919 record a public reading about the Treaty of Graz in the old meeting room.

Following the Northern Water Act in 1963, the council filed a new plan of the town's drains, which may be inspected by appointment.

pages.title: Minutes and Older Papers
pages.content:
MINUTES AND OLDER PAPERS

The minute books of Alderdyke Town Council are held in the tin cabinet behind the clerk's desk. Extracts may be seen during ordinary opening hours.

The earliest volumes in the current cabinet begin after the Treaty of Graz, when the parish boundaries were redrawn against the low fen. Enquiries regarding older vestry books should be directed to the library.

During the Great Wheat Blight in 1933, the council arranged a room for growers to compare what they had seen in their fields.

Papers concerning the Northern Water Act are kept in the lower drawer alongside survey maps and dyke correspondence. More recent minutes concerning roadside measurements and survey work are being transcribed as time allows.

pages.title: The Library Room
pages.content:
ALDERDYKE LIBRARY ROOM

Welcome to our volunteer lending room and archive shelves, situated over the grocer on the high pavement. 

Please note the street stairs are open on Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Saturday mornings only. Do not attempt the inner latch when the blind is drawn downstairs.

Visitors are kindly asked to leave wet umbrellas in the ceramic stand downstairs in the shop passage before coming up, as the paper folders suffer dreadfully from fen damp and drip.

Borrowing is free to all parish residents upon giving a name and road. 

> Members and Register library.ad/members
> Local Papers and Folders library.ad/papers

pages.title: New Members
pages.content:
NEW MEMBERS AND TICKETS

Tickets are made up on card stock once a month and kept in the small grey tin behind the lending stool.

Recent enrolments for the winter quarter:
- T. Crane, Low Road
- J. Finch, Causeway Cottages
- M. Moss, ticket waiting at desk
- S. Pratt, Station Turn

If you are M. Moss, please speak to Ailsa on Thursday. The handwriting on the application slip was very clear but none of the Tuesday volunteers recall handing the form across, nor does anyone remember meeting you on the stairs.

Our cuttings folder on the dissolution of the Pan-Andean Union in 1972 includes a letter sent to an Alderdyke family by a relative abroad.

pages.title: Papers and Cuttings
pages.content:
PAPERS AND CUTTINGS ARCHIVE

The box files are kept on the south wall away from the radiator pipes. Please replace each folder in its numbered slipcase.

Index of special files:
- Alderdyke Fen Drainage Acts (1844-1891), three bundles
- Pumping station ledger (1938-1961), available by request from the locked cupboard
- Alderdyke Parish Survey sheets, hand-ruled
- Dissolution of the Pan-Andean Union (cuttings, 1972)
- Machinery notices and road diversions, ongoing

The old ledger may only be consulted using the flat table near the front window so pages do not buckle.

pages.title: Notice Board
pages.content:
ALDERDYKE NOTICE BOARD

Welcome to the board for Alderdyke and surrounding droveways. Hosted from the repair shed behind the blacksmith.

Please type your message clearly and select the correct heading. We ask again that neighbours do not place personal telephone numbers in the thread titles. Leave your name or house instead, or call in at the counter. Items left over thirty days are cleared by the script.

Active topics this week:

> Thread: Noise after closing time board.ad/forum/t/118
> Thread: West road distances board.ad/forum/t/123
> Thread: Saturday lift board.ad/forum/t/127

Remember to clear your browser cache if threads do not show the latest replies.

pages.title: Noise after closing time
pages.content:
Thread: Noise after closing time

[pencilpot] Did anyone else hear the humming start up again after half twelve last night. It sets the glass rattling on the back dresser until nearly two.
[flatbed] Heard it out by the turn. Like a dry fan turning slow. Stopped at ten past one by my kitchen clock.
[stairshelf] It was running at quarter past midnight when I shut the landing sash. It did not sound like the pumping station at all. The station has a steady stroke.
[fieldnotes] The pumps are ordinary. The rear engines have their own schedule this month and do not take town steam.
[minutesman] There have been three notes left through the council slot regarding the rattle. We have added the hours to the weekly folder.
[spokewill] It was off by twenty to two because I went down the shed for an inner tube and there was only the ditch owls.

pages.title: West road distances
pages.content:
Thread: West road distances

[minutesman] The ditch surveyor puts the white bridge at four hundred and ten yards past the culvert. The surveyor from the south yard measured it at four hundred and thirty-five.
[sidegate] My father always said four hundred paces from the gate to the first plank. He stepped it every autumn before the sheep moved.
[sheetmab] We have printed both numbers in the gazetteer so people may choose. The works surveyor had forty yards more than the council man.
[spokewill] My cyclometer showed forty-two chain on Tuesday morning, but the back tyre was soft. I can ride it again on Friday noon if the wind drops.
[flatbed] The mile post is leaning into the silt anyway. If you measure from the crown it will be shorter than from the ditch side.
[minutesman] Both slips have been posted away for checking. We are told another measurement is due on Friday.

pages.title: Saturday lift
pages.content:
Thread: Saturday lift

[pencilpot] We need the five long trestles shifted from the church hall to the club room before four o'clock for the card drive. The caretaker cannot lift.
[flatbed] I can bring the green Austin flatbed round after dinner. Have someone there with the side door key.
[sidegate] The key is on the hook. Mind the green tarpaulin as it tears easily if caught on the hinge.
[flatbed] Bring some decent sisal. Half-hitches only. If someone ties another bowline like last Michaelmas we shall be there with a pocket knife till dark.
[spokewill] A round turn and two half-hitches never jams even when wet. It is what we use on the cart shafts.
[pencilpot] The cards list is posted up for those who asked:
1st: G. Arber and guest
2nd: M. Moss and partner
3rd: J. Callow
Tables to be wiped before loading please.

pages.title: This Month's Sheet
pages.content:
THIS MONTH'S SHEET

Welcome to the web page for the Alderdyke Sheet. We print on the third Thursday and place copies in the porch, the club and the bakery. The next collection day for paper copies from the back room will be Wednesday the 18th from four until six o'clock.

There is a jumble sale in aid of the mower fund on Saturday week in the hall. Clean clothes and small kitchen pots only, please. No heavy ironware as the tables are tired.

The deadline for handwritten notices for next month is Tuesday noon. Please push them through Mabel Drewe's letterbox folded twice, with your name clear on the back, or pass them to Cora Pell at the club.

> A Note from the Works sheet.ad/works
> Things We Kept Cuttings About sheet.ad/history

pages.title: A Note from the Works
pages.content:
A NOTE FROM THE WORKS

A short note from Hester Quillan reminds us that the field research works is continuing to check its baseline instruments along the north ditch. The low hum heard after midnight from the outbuildings is part of this testing schedule, and the works office states that no interruption to drainage has been announced for the coming week.

Our old cuttings show the pumping station staff discussing the Northern Water Act in 1963 over a photograph taken beside the main dyke. At that time, as now, the station kept to its ordinary hours while outside contractors took their levels.

Friday's measurements will be carried out along the road out as planned, though the works has not yet given the names of the team.

pages.title: Things We Kept Cuttings About
pages.content:
THINGS WE KEPT CUTTINGS ABOUT

A few items from the drawer under the folding table. Mabel Drewe has been sorting through the back bundles from the old parish shed.

Our old cuttings show the pumping station staff discussing the Northern Water Act in 1963 over a photograph taken beside the main dyke. The council ditch survey had only three pages that year, all bound with green tape.

The Sheet's first report on the Copper Coast oil strike in 1975 sits beside an advert for seed potatoes. Several men from the lower fens went north on the train that winter, though most returned before the spring sowing.

When the Calais to Dover bridge opened in 1992, the Sheet printed a local driver's account of the journey. He remarked on the great concrete pillars and the spray coming off the grey channel.

pages.title: St Eda's
pages.content:
ST EDA'S PARISH CHURCH, ALDERDYKE

Welcome to St Eda's. We are a parish church serving Alderdyke and the surrounding fen.

Services are held on Sundays at 8.00 am and 10.30 am, and on Wednesdays at 10.00 am. Evensong is at 6.00 pm on the first and third Sundays of the month.

To find us from Harbour Street, turn south down Church Dyke Bank past the coal yard and follow the gravel path between the willows. Visitors should note that the side gate by the vestry is exceptionally stiff in damp weather. Push firmly against the iron catch with your shoulder and it will open.

Enquiries may be left with Kester Nall.

> Parish Supper steda.ad/supper
> From the Parish Register steda.ad/register

pages.title: Parish Supper
pages.content:
PARISH SUPPER NOTICES

The Michaelmas Parish Supper will take place in the church hall on Thursday at 7.00 pm. All are welcome.

Regarding donated puddings, please leave all pies, tarts, and cold desserts on the slate table behind the scullery door. Do not leave them on the trestles near the coats. To make sure nobody is confused, cold puddings must be put directly onto the slate table behind the scullery door before six o'clock so that the helpers know what has arrived.

The parish register notes a collection of flour and potatoes during the Great Wheat Blight in 1933.

We are grateful to those bringing custard in flasks.

> Parish Register steda.ad/register

pages.title: From the Parish Register
pages.content:
FROM THE PARISH REGISTER

A small selection of transcriptions from the vestry books, prepared by Kester Nall for general interest.

November 1914: After the Ostend Settlement in 1914, St Eda's held a supper for two local men who had been working at a shipyard.

October 1933: In the autumn of this year, forty-eight sacks of potatoes and three stones of mill flour were received into the dry cellar of the porch, for distribution to cottagers during the Great Wheat Blight.

Further excerpts covering the drainage works and churchyard boundary will be typed and added as time allows.

pages.title: Club Home
pages.content:
ALDERDYKE SOCIAL CLUB

Welcome to the official page for the Alderdyke Social Club, established 1904. We are situated opposite the lower ditch track.

Opening hours are Tuesdays and Thursdays from half past seven until eleven, and Saturdays from seven until half past eleven. Members are reminded that the back door sticks in damp weather, particularly when the mist comes off the fen after sundown. Please pull firmly on the brass handle and do not kick the bottom panel, as Cora Pell has only just re-screwed the draught excluder.

New memberships may be proposed on quiz evenings.

pages.title: Thursday Quiz Results
pages.content:
THURSDAY QUIZ RESULTS

Scored by Cora Pell. Eight tables entered for the round of general knowledge and fen curiosities.

First place: The Dyke Cutters with twenty-four points. The team comprised Hollis Ruddock, young Peter, and an M. Moss, although nobody at the table recalls meeting that player prior to the fourth round when the slips were gathered.

Second place: The Parish Row with twenty-two points.

Tie-break question regarding historic dates was avoided as points were clear.

pages.title: Field Works Information
pages.content:
ALDERDYKE FIELD WORKS

The works operates beside the main dyke and the brick pumping station on the south track out of town. We carry out routine soil water observation, culvert levels, and periodic field measurements along the road boundary markers.

Please note that access along the lower gravel road past the brick chimney is restricted while instruments are out on tripods. For enquiries about daily access or visiting the enclosure, ring the caretaker during daytime hours between nine and three on 442.

> Hours and Sound works.ad/hours
> Reading Notes works.ad/readings

pages.title: Hours and Sound
pages.content:
HOURS AND SOUND

Notice to householders along South Dyke. Certain apparatus and underground testing gear may run after midnight during the current survey window. This machinery operates on a low, uneven cycle and should not be mistaken for the regular drainage engine at the pumping station.

Residents who hear a hum or beat are requested to note down the exact minute it commences and how long it persists. Please pass these times to the site office so we can compare them against equipment logs.

New this month: M. Moss has been engaged for morning gate duties and post delivery.

> Main Page works.ad
> Reading Notes works.ad/readings

pages.title: Reading Notes
pages.content:
READING NOTES

A reminder concerning public enquiries about the ditch figures. The leatherbound log books belonging to the original fen pumping station are kept separate in the front store and record only simple pump strokes and water head depths from previous decades.

Current work uses our own loose sheets and ground chains. Distances along the ditch bank have differed from the council surveyor figures, but both charts are now with the outside office for cross-checking. The next set of measurements is due on Friday.

traffic.subject: Friday chain survey
traffic.body:
Dear Hester,

Just looking over the ditch returns before packing up my satchel. Mr Crane's rod survey gives three hundred and forty-two yards between the culvert post and your northern gate, but the slip your office sent over says three hundred and ninety. We have sent both slips to the district assessor in March, but he won't look at them until their committee sits. Who is walking the chain with Mr Crane on Friday morning? You didn't put an initial on the card.

Yours,
Oren

traffic.subject: Re: Friday chain survey
traffic.body:
Oren,

I only look after the stoves and the brasses in the gatehouse now. The board in the lobby just says 'The Observer' against Friday, nine o'clock, same as usual. It might be the relief man from Ely, or it might just be the surveyor from the water board with the brass rod. I will leave the south chain by the boot scraper.

Hester

traffic.subject: St Eda's notices for the Friday Sheet
traffic.body:
Dear Kester,

Do you have the Saturday flower rota? Also, Mrs Finch wants to know if the bell ringing on Wednesday was practice or an occasion. It carried right across the dyke to the washhouse.

Mabel

traffic.subject: Re: St Eda's notices for the Friday Sheet
traffic.body:
Mabel,

It was only young Peter trying the sally after oiling the gudgeon pins. There was no service. My gran said the bell was rung here for the Treaty of Graz in 1919, though she always added that the rope broke afterwards. We have only had the small four in use since.

Rota is: Miss Teversham (chancel), Mrs Clout (porch). I have written them in the vestry ledger already.

Kester

traffic.subject: Inner tube / pump
traffic.body:
Hollis,

I found that heavy 28-inch tube in the crate under the bench. You can have it for two shillings or a couple of your leeks if they're up. I noticed you drove out towards the pumping station at six. Did you get past the second bend? My boy says the road looks terribly long this week.

Wilf

traffic.subject: Re: Inner tube / pump
traffic.body:
Wilf,

I only went as far as the sluice cottages to turn the Austin round. Nobody ever seems to go right out along that west road past the works and the station; it just seems to run into the haze by the low droves and you never meet a car coming back the other way. I will bring two leeks round tomorrow for the tube.

Hollis

traffic.subject: Old drainage parcel map (1884)
traffic.body:
Oren,

I pulled out the cloth-backed map of the Forty-Foot drain you asked after. It does show an old coal wharf and an inlet marked 'The Harbour' where the works yard stands now, back when they brought the fuel in by barge. But there's no road marked to the west at all, just a drove road ending at the peat cut.

Ailsa

traffic.subject: Whist drive scores and raffle
traffic.body:
Mabel,

For the parish page: Whist winners were Mrs Teversham (first) and Arthur Parn (booby). The raffle raised fourteen pounds ten for the roof guttering.

Also, on the patron list on the club noticeboard, who is M. Moss? The name has been neatly inked under 'Life Members' between Mr Gedge and Mrs Vawser for about ten years, but nobody at the committee has ever seen him pay a subscription or take a glass of shandy.

Cora

traffic.subject: Re: Whist drive scores and raffle
traffic.body:
Cora,

I shall put the scores in the middle column. About M. Moss: old Mr Crane once told me that name was already on the brass board when the social club moved out of the old chapel rooms in forty-eight. He thought Moss might have been an inspector for the ditch dykes who lived over at Prickwillow, but nobody remembers him.

Mabel

traffic.subject: Re: Old drainage parcel map (1884)
traffic.body:
Ailsa,

Thank you for looking. The Harbour is what they still call the slipway behind the boiler house, though it's all dry nettles now. What bothers the parish meeting is that the works ledger from 1922 calls the boundary four hundred paces, but our new tape measure makes it four hundred and fifty. Things shouldn't stretch out across the peat like that.

Oren

traffic.subject: Thump in the night
traffic.body:
Hester,

Was that your compound engine kicking off at twenty past twelve last night? It sounded like an uneven three-beat, tap-tap... pause... tap, not the steady churning the pumping station usually has when the water is high in the cut.

Wilfred

traffic.subject: Re: Thump in the night
traffic.body:
Wilfred,

It wasn't the pumps. The district engineer had the steam cut off at four yesterday afternoon. Whatever makes that tapping comes from the shed beyond the gravel pit, which isn't mine to oil. They had three lanterns burning out there until three in the morning, but the gates were locked from the inside.

Hester

traffic.subject: Friday dart match transport
traffic.body:
Hollis,

Can you take four in the back of the van to Sutton St Edmund on Friday? Wilfred says his chain snapped on the tandem so he won't be cycling, and young Peter wants a lift.

Cora

traffic.subject: Re: Friday dart match transport
traffic.body:
Cora,

Yes, if they don't mind sitting on sacks of bran. I need to leave by seven though, because we can't take the west road through the fen—nobody ever goes that way, it's all potholes and you never know where the ditch begins—so I'll have to go round by the causeway.

Hollis

traffic.subject: Grave plots / ditch side
traffic.body:
Oren,

When the council chainmen do the ditch boundary on Friday, could they keep their boots off the nettle bank behind the old churchyard? The soil there is soft and the stone for Ephraim Moss (d. 1891) is already leaning towards the water.

Kester

traffic.subject: Re: Grave plots / ditch side
traffic.body:
Kester,

I will tell them. Is Ephraim Moss any relation to the M. Moss on the club list? Ailsa was asking about him only yesterday because of a post card from 1931 that turned up behind the library shelves addressed to 'M. Moss, The Fen Office, Alderdyke'.

Oren

traffic.subject: Re: Grave plots / ditch side
traffic.body:
Oren,

No, Ephraim died a bachelor without kin in the parish. The baptismal ledger doesn't have an M. Moss anywhere between 1870 and 1910. He must be someone belonging to the works who never took church fellowship here.

Kester

traffic.subject: Library hours note
traffic.body:
Mabel,

Could you put a tiny box in the Sheet? 'Alderdyke Reading Room will close at four on Friday instead of five, to allow the volunteer to attend the boundary viewing at the dyke.'

We had eleven people in on Tuesday, which is very good for November.

Ailsa

traffic.subject: Re: Library hours note
traffic.body:
Ailsa,

I will squeeze it right under the poultry prices. Are you going out to the three-mile stone for the viewing? Wilfred told me the council chain made the stone three miles and two furlongs, while the works surveyor made it three miles exactly. It seems very strange that a stone could move forty chains into the grass without someone noticing the turf broken.

Mabel

traffic.subject: Re: Library hours note
traffic.body:
Mabel,

Yes, I want to see Mr Crane lay the brass rods. Old maps call that corner 'The Harbour Dyche' because of the broad turn for the turf boats. It doesn't move, of course, but the peat rises and falls with the wet. Although they say the ditch itself has been bone dry since October.

Ailsa

traffic.subject: Forum bulletin board page
traffic.body:
Oren,

I have updated the council minutes page on the dial-up board. There were two spelling mistakes in the surveyor's memo about the culvert. I put 'discrepancy' with one p. Let me know if the parish clerk wants his telephone number listed or just the post box.

Wilfred

traffic.subject: Re: Forum bulletin board page
traffic.body:
Wilfred,

Just the post box, thank you. If we put the telephone, people ring during tea whenever the night engine starts up. Mrs Pell rang me three times last week about the hum rattling the tumblers on her dresser.

Oren

traffic.subject: Empty crates behind the hall
traffic.body:
Hester,

There are three green wooden crates stacked by our coal bunker with 'F.R.W. Alderdyke' stencilled on them. Did your lorry drop them by mistake? They are very heavy and smell strongly of paraffin or machine tallow.

Cora

traffic.subject: Re: Empty crates behind the hall
traffic.body:
Cora,

Leave them be until Friday. The lorry didn't drop them; they were set down by the three men who came off the night shift at four. They contain iron weights for checking the balance on the bog-levers. I will get Hollis to shift them with his sack-barrow if they are in your way for darts.

Hester

traffic.subject: Re: Empty crates behind the hall
traffic.body:
Hester,

I can shift them tomorrow noon before dinner. Don't let them leave them in the puddle though, the timber will rot out. Is the works road open past the bridge tomorrow? I need to get some gravel from the pit.

Hollis

traffic.subject: Re: Empty crates behind the hall
traffic.body:
Hollis,

The gate is open until half-past two, then they have the red disc up while they adjust the wire. If the red disc is hanging, don't drive in, just wait on the gravel turn.

Hester

traffic.subject: Parish bundle 1898
traffic.body:
Ailsa,

Did you return the parcel of drainage receipts from 1898 to the vestry cupboard? The bottom shelf has a gap between the tithe book and the choir register.

Kester

traffic.subject: Re: Parish bundle 1898
traffic.body:
Kester,

I brought them back on Monday afternoon. They are wrapped in brown paper inside the tin box marked 'Sluice & Dyke'. There is an odd note pinned to the back of the ledger by an 'M. Moss' from December 1904, approving eight pence for tallow, but no address given.

Ailsa

traffic.subject: Re: Parish bundle 1898
traffic.body:
Ailsa,

I have found the box. Thank you. It was behind the hassocks. That Moss name again—it seems he signed for everything between the queen's death and the great frost, and then simply evaporated into the peat.

Kester

traffic.subject: Survey article for the back page
traffic.body:
Oren,

Can I write: 'The Council and the Field Works are jointly reviewing the west boundary chainage this coming Friday'? Or will that upset the surveyor from March?

Mabel

traffic.subject: Re: Survey article for the back page
traffic.body:
Mabel,

Better to say 'routine measurement of the outfall drove'. Don't mention the fifty-yard discrepancy. People get superstitious about the ground moving under their orchards, when it is almost certainly just Mr Crane's chain being stretched by the boy pulling too hard at the corners.

Oren

traffic.subject: Quiz questions for next Tuesday
traffic.body:
Cora,

I have twelve questions ready for the local round. One is: 'What was the original name of the field research works before 1920?' (Answer: Alderdyke Steam Drainage Trust). Another is: 'How many culverts cross the west road between the church and the parish end?' Though we might have to argue about that one after Friday's recount!

Wilfred

traffic.subject: Re: Quiz questions for next Tuesday
traffic.body:
Wilfred,

Don't put the culvert question in, Arthur and George will spend forty minutes shouting over their mild about the stone pipe by the smithy. Put something about the church clock instead.

Cora

traffic.subject: Friday key
traffic.body:
Oren,

Just to let you know, the works office will be locked on Friday morning, but the wicket gate to the ditch bank will be on the latch from eight o'clock. If the March clerk arrives before Mr Crane, tell him to wait by the rain gauge and not to go into the gravel bay.

Hester

traffic.subject: Re: Friday key
traffic.body:
Hester,

Understood. We will meet at the gate at nine sharp with the linen tape and the ledger. Let's hope the mist stays off the fen so we can take a proper sight through the glass.

Oren

traffic.subject: Noise again
traffic.body:
Hester,

It has just started up again. Twenty-eight minutes to nine, a steady low double-knock from the direction of your pump pit, like a heavy iron piston taking stroke in water. It isn't loud, but it makes the tea in the cup tremble. Are you sure all the valves are shut down?

Wilf

hqMail.subject: Assignment 0xBB6F (ALDERDYKE): field brief
hqMail.body:
Agent,

You have been assigned Reality 0xBB6F, local name ALDERDYKE. Alderdyke is a small fen town with a council, library, church, social club, newsletter, pumping station and field research works. Desk 9 estimates it at five to seven weeks old. The inhabitants (non-canonical) will report a longer history, as their memories have been generated to remain consistent with the local state.

Reconciliation requires three findings. Enter them together on the HQ Console and inject the reverse seed.

1. Divergence. The year of the latest canonical event that the reality verifiably records. Your Canon Reference lists canonical events by year. A record counts when two independent sources in the reality agree on it.
2. Apotheosis. The depth to which the local intelligence (designation pending) can interfere with this workstation, on a scale of 1 to 5. It is assessed from what it does. It may imitate an interference it cannot perform, and may conceal one it can.
3. Inferiority. The extent of the reality, graded Class I (smallest) to Class V. Inhabitants believe their world to be complete and cannot report its extent unprompted. It is established only by an inhabitant who travels to its limit. Measured along a road from the town: Class I under 2 miles; Class II, 2 to 10; Class III, 10 to 40; Class IV, 40 to 150; Class V, beyond.

A wrong injection is detected by the local intelligence at once, discloses the values entered, and locks the console for twelve minutes.

You have been placed in the reality as M. Moss <moss.m@board.ad>. A small number of local records refer to you. No inhabitant has met you.

Your workstation credential is the address above and the words HARBOUR and LEDGER. Under Security Instruction 4 these words are withheld from all agent input and will appear as apostrophes.

Form 77-R will be filed automatically at the close of the assignment. If you have not viewed the orientation film, a copy has been placed on your desktop by Training.

D. Okonkwo-Vance
Desk 14, Canonical Restoration
